utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed there was a translation issue to be raised before we start. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have an updated translation provided to us by the Prosecution for Exhibit D1280, and we ask permission to upload it into e-court with doc ID 0673-0221ET.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It doesn't ring immediately a bell to me, but if the parties agree that it's a better translation, Mr. Misetic, the issue was -- you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We had provided a partial translation of the document. I believe Mr. Carrier wants to use it in his cross-examination, and he has provided a full translation, and we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- then leave is grant to upload a new translation for Exhibit D1280. Any other matter? If not, could the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Juric. Perhaps needless --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps needless to say, but you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Carrier. Mr. Carrier is counsel for the Prosecution. You'll find him to your right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Brigadier Juric.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could we please have document 65 ter 7587 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Brigadier Juric, while this is coming up on the screen in front of you, yesterday Judge Orie asked you some questions about your area of responsibility, for your co-ordinator role as assigned by General Lausic, and references there are T-27421 and following. And yesterday you said that the area was the Split Military District, and you also mentioned that the area was dynamic, in the sense that it changed as additional areas were liberated by the Croatian Army. And if you could just focus on the map in front of you, Brigadier Juric, I'm wondering if at the time that you were sent to Knin, if you were aware that normally the northern border of the Split Military District area of operations corresponded roughly with the solid yellow line that's shown on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And perhaps we could just close in a little bit. It's the bottom half of this map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please zoom in a bit more? I spoke about the zone of responsibility of the Military District of Split. Well, that area of responsibility was based on the area that was under Croatian control. I am not aware, in detail, of the borders between the Split Military District and the neighbour on the left side, that is to say, the newly liberated areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Okay. So given your answer, looking at this map, when you say "left side," you mean the northern part of Croatia, meaning above the yellow line; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know if it's above the yellow line or where it is on the map. I'm telling you that I wasn't aware of where the line of separation was between the Split Military District and the left side of the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So I take it, then, you wouldn't be able to confirm whether or not -- or what the northern border of the Split Military District would have been on the 6th of August or the 14th of August, 1995. You wouldn't really know precisely?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could have this map marked as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could have it MFI'd. We just got it a few minutes ago before we came in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and you'd like to see what we find on it before you express your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that this would be the same for the other Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I wonder if it adds anything at all, Your Honour, as the witness didn't speak to the map or adopt any part of it. So in that sense, making it an exhibit I'm not sure helps the Court in any way. I see that some of the information already comes from other documents on it, and it's not the witness's map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document will be marked for identification. Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2715, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2715 keeps that status, MFI, for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Madam Registrar, if we could please have Exhibit D267 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Brigadier Juric, what's going to come up on the screen in front of you is General Lausic's 2 August 1995 order in relation to preparations of military police units to perform military police tasks in the area of responsibility of the Croatian Army military districts during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry, D267. And if we could turn to page 4 in the English, please, and the top of page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Brigadier Juric, under this order from General Lausic, you were appointed to assist in commanding and organising the activities of the 72nd and 73rd Military Police Battalions. This is located at item 10 of his order, and it also says that the commanders of these two battalions shall be subordinated to you. Brigadier Juric, when you were briefed about your role as the Military Police Administration co-ordinator for Operation Storm by General Lausic, you were told that the military police would be given tasks by the military district commanders; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Your Honours, I explained yesterday, in response to your question, what my role and task were. When I spoke yesterday, I never mentioned, and I never mentioned it today either, that the military police would receive orders from the commander of the military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Brigadier Juric, yesterday His Honour was reminding you that you gave -- you were interviewed by the investigators from the Prosecution in March 2002. And for reference, at paragraph 4, page 2, Your Honour, you were recorded as telling the investigators that the military police would be given tasks by the military district commanders. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, I spoke to the investigator. However, I never saw the record. Afterwards, I never checked the record, and I have no idea what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: The question wasn't about whether you checked the record. The question was whether or not you said that.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no, because commanders of military districts in this specific case did not issue orders to officers who were sent to the ground by the chief of the Administration of Military Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: They would be issuing orders to the Military Police Battalion commanders; isn't that fair?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As prescribed in the rules, the commanders --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer slower, notes the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer, but speak a bit slower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In accordance with the rules on the establishment of the military police, the commanders of military districts were superior to commanders of battalions of the military police in the daily system of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise. Could we check the interpretation of the last portion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please slowly repeat the last part of your answer. You said that in accordance with the rules on the establishment of the military police, the commanders of military districts were superior to commanders of battalions of the military police, and then you said something about command and control, or could you please repeat that last portion of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The system of daily operative command, management and command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And perhaps if we just look down in the same document that's on the screen in front of you, item number 12, Brigadier Juric, there's a heading called "Commanding and reporting system." That indicates that daily operational chain of command for the commanders of the military police battalions was given to the military district commanders, as you just said. And then if we turn the page in English, there also the Military Police Battalion commanders would be reporting in writing in -- at briefings on a daily basis to the military district commander. Is that consistent with what you just described, in terms of the daily operative command?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yesterday, I also explained that from the moment when the military police was established on the basis of the Rules on Establishment, every commander of the Military Police Battalion had to provide daily reports to commanders of military districts about what happened over the past 24 or 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, in fact, yesterday, Brigadier Juric, when you were asked about -- by Judge Orie about reporting between HV operational commanders and military police, and this is at T-27438, there may have been a little confusion, but what you did was you referred to the customary practice of the military police, and then I'll quote you about what you said. You said: "The highest-ranking commander in an area of responsibility was the operative commander, was supposed to receive daily operational reports from military police units, and that had, indeed, covered all the developments in the corresponding area over the period of 24 hours. Also, those commanders are supposed to be present at the briefings that operative commanders, in their respective areas of responsibility, held. At those briefings, they were supposed to receive certain information -- or, rather, they were supposed to be briefed, they were supposed to provide briefings to others." And just to be clear, when you say "operative commander" here, you're referring to the HV commander with operational control over the military police unit; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier Juric, in terms of the tasks that can be assigned by the military district commander to Military Police Battalion commanders, those would be to issue orders relating to military police units performing regular military police tasks?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to object at this point. I believe the Chamber's -- this is now outside the scope of the Chamber's examination, and now we are getting into what, in the e-mail, was indicated that the Chamber would not get into, which is the functioning and structure of the military police in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe there are a number of questions from the Bench yesterday about the ability to issue orders and what those orders would consist of, and this witness talked about that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you could point me to the record as to the specific questions so that I know how this arises out of the Bench's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Well, the whole last section regarding General Cermak, for instance. I believe that starts around page 60 on yesterday's transcript. I can find the actual page, but I -- I don't know if Your Honour remembers those questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do remember some of my questions, yes, Mr. Carrier, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I mean, obviously those questions were specific to General Cermak, and I think Mr. Carrier's questions are specific to General Gotovina at this point. So if he wants to focus on General Cermak, that's fine, but I believe the Bench's questions were very specific as to General Cermak yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, you are at the edge of where you could go. Don't stay there too long, because you might fall off. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'll proceed with caution, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: If I could just read the question to you again. Brigadier Juric, in terms of the tasks that can be assigned by the military district commander to Military Police Battalion commanders, that would include orders relating to military police units performing regularly -- regular military police tasks. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, that is what is prescribed in the rules for the work of the military police. The daily operative orders are issued by the commander of the military district where members of the military police, in accordance with their powers, can give support to the carrying out of the task issued by the commander to his own units.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm off the subject now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: If we just turn now to the appointment again, your appointment, Brigadier Juric.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Madam Registrar, if we could please have Exhibit D268 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Brigadier Juric, what's coming up on the screen is a document that you looked at yesterday when you testified. And if we could please -- once it comes up on the screen, I'll ask you to focus on item number 1. I'll just wait until it comes up. Now, looking at item number 1, you, along with some other Military Police Administration officers, were sent to the 72nd Military Police Battalion Forward Command Post, and at the bottom of the page in English, your name's mentioned, and then there's a list of assigned tasks. It goes on to the next page. It's all on page 1 in the B/C/S. But if you could just take a moment to review that. I know you did yesterday, but just have a chance to review it again, and I'll ask you a couple of questions. Just let me know when you're done looking at it.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead. You can put your question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. Is it fair to say that General Lausic's orders, dated the 2nd of August, 1995, which we just looked at, did not appoint you to take over or replace the command role that was occupied by either of the Military Police Battalion commanders, the 72nd or the 73rd, in respect of their battalions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have already explained. I was not appointed as a commander of -- the commander of any of those units. The procedure to appoint people is prescribed, and only those officers who are in command duties, who have been appointed commanders, are, indeed, commanders. And that's why I said that I was just a co-ordinator who co-ordinated, directed, and channeled certain tasks and the way those tasks were carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it also fair to say that your appointment under these orders of General Lausic did nothing to change or inhibit the ongoing daily operational subordination of the commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, Major Budimir, to the Split Military District commander, Colonel General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I've already said, we arrived with a group of officers from the military police to help link up and co-ordinate the work and activities of the military police in that territory, and all -- every officer in the group had his own tasks and covered a certain area of work that they were most familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Brigadier Juric, yesterday you said that the garrison commander -- sorry, as garrison commander, General Cermak had the right to issue tasks to the military police, in terms of implementing - and you gave some examples - security details, checks, and similar things. And you were asked by Judge Orie what the basis was on which General Cermak had the right or authority to issue such tasks to the military police. For reference, that's transcript page 27457 and following on the next page. You answered, Brigadier Juric, and I'll just quote you again: "Duties, tasks, and whatever the military police had, in keeping with the rules, every officer had the right to issue requirements and tasks that the military police then implemented. If they were in accordance with the area of work and the authorities of the military police, in that case the military police were duty-bound to carry them out in the prescribed -- in the way prescribed by the scope of their work." Brigadier Juric, I would like to show you a document and then follow up on the answer that you gave to Judge Orie.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: If I could please have Exhibit D1280. This is the document, Your Honour, with the now complete translation. And, Madam Registrar, when you get that on the screen --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Brigadier Juric, you'll see that this is a 3rd December 1995 order issued by General Lausic regarding establishing the areas of responsibility of military police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Madam Registrar, if we could please go to page 7 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Brigadier Juric, if you could focus your attention on item number 7 of this order, which indicates that the 72nd Military Police Battalion shall carry out military and police tasks in the area of operations or area of responsibility of the Split Military District and the Southern Front. It goes on. The next paragraph down from that in item 7 indicates that the 72nd Military Police Battalion commander shall be subordinated to the Split Military District commander, in terms of daily operational command. And the next paragraph down from that, you'll see, indicates that: "In matters of daily operational command, platoon and company commanders who are outside of the command headquarters of the 72nd Military Police Battalion Command are subordinated to the commanders of the HV garrisons or to the most senior HV commander in their area of responsibility." Now, Brigadier Juric, is this item number 7 of this order in keeping with the rules that you mentioned that form a basis for General Cermak's authority to issue orders and tasks to military police units as a garrison commander at the relevant time in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe I'm not competent to talk about this. I don't know what General Cermak's authorities were and what they were based on. I don't know what he did and how he did it. However, in terms of bullet point 7, I explained that yesterday, and I said that every operative commander had the right to issue orders to the military police active in his area of responsibility and that the unit commander was duty-bound to carry out the order if it was within the scope of the police -- military police duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, Brigadier Juric.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: If we could please have Exhibit P881 on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Brigadier Juric, what will come up on the screen is a 5th of August, 1995, order issued by General Lausic in respect of the establishment of military police units in the newly liberated areas of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just while we're waiting, the document was introduced by Mr. Carrier with an inaccurate date. It's the 3rd of December, 1994, not 1995, is the date on the document from General Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I apologise. If I said "1995," I did mean 1994. I appreciate the correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Brigadier Juric, this is the document I just described to you, the 5th of August order.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Madam Registrar, if we could -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Brigadier Juric, if you could focus on item 1.5. That's, in English, on page 1, where General Lausic ordered that the 72nd Military Police Battalion establish a military police company in Knin. And just for the record, so you're aware, this Chamber has received evidence that that actually happened on the 5th of August, 1995, at about noon, that that MP company was formed. If we could turn the page in English, please, to page 2, and the B/C/S to page 2. And, Brigadier Juric, if you could focus your attention on item number 7 of this order, which indicates that: "For the execution of daily operations, the commanders of the newly established military police units shall be subordinated to the most senior HV commander in their respective zone of responsibility." Which, I believe, IS consistent with what you've been saying so far, is that right, about operational commands?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Now, in August 1995, Brigadier Juric, setting aside the fact that General Gotovina was the overall commander of the military district, it's true, isn't it, that your understanding was that General Cermak was the most senior HV commander in Knin at the relevant time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, General Cermak was the commander of the Knin Garrison, and as far as I know, he did not have operative authority over the units of the Croatian Army that were deployed in Knin in any capacity. He did not have any authority over the installations that were used by members of the Croatian Army in Knin. I can't tell you, and I've already told you that, I can't tell you what exactly were the tasks and duties of the garrison commander there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Irrespective of the operational role of General Cermak, your understanding was that he was the -- other than General Gotovina, he was the most senior-ranked military person in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, that's a very misleading question, if I may say so, and the Court knows fully the background to this. It may be my learned friend's inexperience with the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, you can ask the witness whether he's aware of the rank held by General Cermak, and you can ask whether he knows of any others having higher ranks. The issue is clear that the Chamber is mainly assisted by questions where it appears that facts, rather than intertwined half conclusions, are dealt with by the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry. Just for some direction from the Bench, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we can -- do you know what the rank of General Cermak was at the time, Mr. Juric? Could you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. General Cermak had the rank of colonel general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber, of course, has a lot of evidence on ranks of others, and what that means, Mr. Carrier, is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm grateful. I take Your Honour's line on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier Juric, you were aware, during August 1995, that -- or as far as you could remember, General Cermak was receiving regular reports about the military police in Knin; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we establish a foundation for that, for that question, Your Honour. With respect to my learned friend, I don't know what he's doing there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that depending on the answer of the witness, that you'll take him through further evidence which the Chamber has received, Mr. Carrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: At least his -- at least evidence that's not in evidence, but that was referred to during Your Honour's examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Under those circumstances, Mr. Kay, the question is put to the witness, and Mr. Carrier will not just leave it to that, but will take us to further evidence on the matter. Please proceed, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry, Brigadier Juric, for the interruption, but you were aware, during August 1995, that at least as far as you could remember, General Cermak was receiving --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, the witness hasn't said he can remember anything. That's the point with a misleading question in that form. The witness has not said he can remember that in that way, and to put a question like that is designed to lead a witness down the path that is misleading, with respect. And the Court knows the evidence in this case, and what has been able to be put into evidence, and what doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, you can ask whether the witness was aware. That would be a more neat and clean question. And to say, Are you aware, at least as far as you could remember, is highly suggestive. Under the present circumstances, where no foundation has yet been laid, I think it's better to refrain from that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Brigadier Juric, you were aware that General Cermak was receiving regular reports about the work of the military police in Knin; isn't that fair?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'm just taking you back to your interview with the Prosecution investigators in March 2002, where you're recorded as saying that as far as you could remember, General Cermak was getting regular reports about the work of the military police in Knin. Does that refresh your memory at all? Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Yesterday, I said that I had not checked how units sent their daily reports through daily operative channels that had been established far before. I don't remember to this very day that I saw a single report sent by the military police unit to General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, needless to ask your attention for the difference in language. Getting regular reports about the work of the military police is not exactly the same of getting regular reports from members of --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I don't have any more questions, Your Honour. I take your point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And I literally don't have any more questions. I'm done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You literally have no more questions, yes. Mr. Juric, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Misetic, at least if he can find a lectern. Otherwise, he'll refrain from cross-examination. He has found one, so you'll be cross-examined by Mr. Misetic. Mr. Misetic is counsel for Mr. Gotovina, as you may be aware of. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Brigadier Juric.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First, let me follow up with some of the questions you were asked this morning, first dealing with the northern boundary of your zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go, Madam Registrar, to Exhibit P887, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And Brigadier Juric, this is an order from General Lausic on the 5th of August. And if you look on the first page in point 1.4, you'll see that a platoon of the military police is formed in Gracac, but it's from the 71st Military Police Battalion. It's correct, isn't it, that you were not responsible for the 71st Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct. The 71st Battalion was not in the area of responsibility. Another team of officers covered that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And that would be the team led by Colonel Kosic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This morning, you were also asked a question at transcript page 8, lines 10 to 12. Just one moment, please. The question was phrased in a way that says the HV commander had operational control over the military police. Isn't it correct that, more specifically, he had -- he was able to issue daily operational tasks to the military police, to be very precise?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The question that was posed to you by Mr. Carrier earlier this morning had embedded in it the presumption that the HV commanders had operational control over the military police, and I just want to be clear that that relates to Article 9 of the Rules of the Military Police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that it relates to Article 9, but, yes, in the rules it does explain how this was done. I'm not 100 per cent sure that it would be Article 9. I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And pursuant to General Lausic's orders, starting with the 2nd of August, the military police was subordinated to the military district commanders in fulfilling daily operational tasks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to go back, Brigadier Juric, to questions that were put to you by the Bench yesterday. You'll recall --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is referring back to Exhibit P1193, page 9 in the English, page 7 in the B/C/S. And, Madam Registrar, if we could call that up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You'll recall this is a report from Captain Grancaric to you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's something wrong with my screen. I can't see the Croatian translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that it's still being uploaded to be visible on your screen. Let's just take a while, because I see that the Croatian part is still the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In Croatian, it's page 7 of 19. That's it, now the bottom paragraph in Croatian. And in English, it is the first translation -- the first English translation, page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Major Juric -- I'm sorry. Brigadier Juric, you'll recall you were shown this by Judge Orie yesterday about: "During the searches we have found five to six dead bodies, and then we informed the security services as well as the services in charge of the clearing up of the terrain. Considering the shortness of time passed since our entrance into the city, we assumed that these were people of Croatian ethnicity who had been killed by Chetniks." My first question: Brigadier Juric, when you received a report like this, would you have had reason to think that proper procedures would not be followed in a case where Croatian victims had been discovered in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if I could have on the screen, please, 65 ter 1D3066.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Brigadier Juric, this is now a criminal report regarding an incident similar to the one described in the report of Captain Grancaric. It's a criminal report against a Nikola Kresovic - if we turn the page, please - committing a war crime, it says. If we turn the page in Croatian as well. It says: "There is reasonable suspicion that Kresovic, Nikola, committed the criminal offence of war crime against the civilian population, against Zrilic, Zorka; Beslic, Vlado; and Beslic, Stana. On 5 August 1995, at an unspecified time, most probably in the early-morning hours immediately prior to the entry of the military police forces of the Republic of Croatia into Benkovac and its liberation, the reported Kresovic, Nikola, using a 7.62-millimetre calibre firearm, make unknown, killed the following persons in their family homes in Benkovac ..." The next paragraph says: "After having murdered the aforesaid persons, the reported person, together with other insurgent citizens of Serb nationality, left Benkovac, or rather the Republic of Croatia, and moved to the area of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina under Serb control." It is signed by Mr. Kardum. If we go two pages further, please, there's also a record of an on-site investigation having been done, with an investigating judge having been called, the district attorney, et cetera. Now, Brigadier Juric, when you received the report from Captain Grancaric, you would have assumed that, in fact, this would have been the procedure that was followed upon the discovery of these bodies; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. Yesterday, in answering a number of questions, I provided a similar answer, and I said that I was absolutely sure that the procedure would be followed, irrespective of the allegations or anything that the recording clerk may have recorded or put on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I tender 65 ter 1D3066 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D2023.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D2023 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Brigadier Juric, I want to turn our attention to a different topic that was covered with you yesterday, and this is reporting about looting as well as reporting to the military commanders. And if we could first turn our attention to 65 ter 5807, please. This is a report of the 7th of August sent to you by the commander of the 5th Company of the 72nd MP Battalion, Captain Janjic. And you can see that starting in paragraph 2, he reports to you about items having been seized and equipment having been seized, and receipts for the temporary seized items have been issued, and it talks about who some of the soldiers are. If we go to point 4 -- could we turn the page in English, please. It talks about the members of the 7th Guards Brigade of the HV having items seized. The next paragraph talks about a soldier in a Toyota truck with HV plates being stopped, inspected: "During the inspection, a large quantity of technical goods was present. Orlovic made away from the check-point without permission. He did not stop. The offender's military ID card and the vehicle worksheet are at the Vrlika barrier check-point premises." It talks about another incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to show him a series of documents, so I'd like to ask that 65 ter 5807 be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D2024.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could have Exhibit D868 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, this is a report of the 8th of August. It's a report, I believe, that covers not only the 8th, but the period prior to that as well, and it itemises some of the things that have been seized at the check-points. And I note, again, and I ask you to pay attention to the fact that this is the 5th Company, Knin -- sorry, Sinj. There's a -- we'll have to have that translation corrected. It includes technical equipment, TV sets, Sanyo players, cassette players, VHS videos. And if we flip through it, there's 222 items seized, according to this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President -- sorry. Madam Registrar, if we could have 65 ter 2748 on the screen, please. This is another report from IZM Vrlika, itemising additional items seized at check-points that include electronic equipment like TV sets, tractors, radio-cassette players, et cetera. Mr. President, I ask that 65 ter 2748 be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D2025, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D2025 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if I could have 65 ter 1D3064, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, just for my information, at this moment you apparently are establishing that the military police took action against what may appear as being looting, in view of the -- that was not the core of my questioning, just for you to be aware of. I didn't say that it didn't happen. I didn't say that the military police -- what I focused on was the way in which it was reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And that's what I'm going to get to, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then that's -- then I'll wait and see how it develops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, this is a report about tractors -- three tractors being seized at a check-point. When the persons driving them couldn't show documents -- proper documentation, they were seized from members of the HV on 7 August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this exhibit, 65 ter 1D0364, be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, I take it, Mr. Carrier. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D2026, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, this is the last one, 65 ter 1D3065. It is a statement that was taken from one HV member suspected of having a cultivator that did not belong to him, and this is his statement describing the military police patrol coming upon him, asking for paperwork. When he didn't have it, he was taken to the forward command post. Mr. President, I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, from what I see from you, you have no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Well, actually, on this -- this point, I'm just trying to confirm -- if it can be marked as MFI for now. I want to just check what the -- I know there's a lot of traffic on the whole Official Note concept, so I just wanted to confirm before I register no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's not an Official Note, Mr. President. It's actually -- it says it's a statement, I guess, of -- in the person's voice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Official Notes are, I think, often not signed by the person from whom a statement is taken, whereas this statement is signed by the person from whom it was taken, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'm just checking that, but I was looking at the description which calls it an Official Note. So if I could just have one moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, that was just in e-court. Someone described it as an Official Note, but the title of the document is a record of taking a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Often, Mr. Carrier, we find "Official Note" in the heading of document, where here it reads "Record of taking a statement."

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: In the Croatian version, I can't even see the heading. I'm just trying to be cautious, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that those who translated it must have been able to read it, perhaps, in a better copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: If there is a better copy, perhaps that could be uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, you can see the ERN number, that we got it from the OTP, so that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can find a better copy, Mr. Carrier, you receive leave to upload it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be MFI'd, but not for very long. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D2027, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And keeps that status for a short while. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier Juric, I want to now show you a report. This is P1134, Madam Registrar. And if we could go to page 4 in the English, and page 4 in the Croatian as well, please. Now, in paragraph 9 of this report, which is the 10th of August, and it's a report of the SIS, it says: "At the very beginning, war booty was not collected in an organised manner. Each unit collected it individually, and some HV members took household appliances, cars and such-like. Most of the items were confiscated from them at VP check-points. In some cases, the VP had to do it by force. A group of armed members of the 7th Guards Brigade requested that the 5th Sinj Company return the confiscated goods to them." Now, Brigadier Juric, is it your recollection that with respect to the items that had been taken in places like Knin, that most of the items had, in fact, ultimately been seized by the military police at check-points?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, Your Honours. Members of the military police at check-points stopped all vehicles of members of the Croatian Army and took away all objects that were not part of military equipment or if the persons involved did not have proper documentation for the said objects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's now look at -- after having looked at these reports, let's look at some of the reporting that was discussed both with the Trial Chamber yesterday and in the Prosecution's cross-examination of you today. You'll recall that you have testified about reporting to the operational HV commanders would have continued along the standard practice of reporting that had existed prior to Operation Storm; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, could I ask clarification of one of the previous answers. The question put to you was whether it was your recollection that with respect to the items that had been taken in places like Knin, that most of the items had, in fact, ultimately been seized by the military police at the check-points. Now, if I understand the items that had been taken to be the items that had been taken from apartments, from wherever, taken from individuals, a judgement that most of these items were ultimately seized by the military police suggests that you had a good knowledge of the total number of items taken. Could you explain how you could tell us whether what was seized by the military police was 10 per cent of what had been -- and I now use the word in non-technical terms, whether that was 10 per cent of the looted goods, or 90 per cent of the looted goods, or 30 per cent of the looted goods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in response to the question put to me, I said that at blockade check-points, the military police stopped all members and seized all goods for which they didn't have proper documentation. I did not say whether these goods, if we are to call it that, belonged to the area or the town of Knin or wherever. We can only talk about what was done at the check-points themselves. Actually, check-points were put up in an attempt to seal off the entire zone. I cannot tell you now with certainty at which check-point how many goods were taken. And when certificates were written up, I don't know whether it was stated from where the said goods came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. This clearly explains the problem. You're asking for a judgement on whether most of these items were then seized, whereas the witness starts saying, Yes, and then explains what they did at the check-points, and which does not allow for any final conclusions on whether most of them were seized or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- if I can just explain my position. I was quoting from a report of the 10th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine, but your question was phrased in a way which went far beyond that. I read the relevant places, like Knin, goods taken. It leaves a lot of questions are open, such as, What was the total quantity of goods that were stolen? How many of those who had taken those goods were stopped at check-points? How many circumvented check-points? What may have been missed in inspecting the cars, for example? If golden rings would have been stolen, you would more easily accept that they would have been missed in the inspection of the cars, compared to refrigerators, for example, which you'll not easily --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll explore it, then. I have an answer to that but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what I'm saying is that -- of course, you can explore that and say, Do you think that you missed rings, and then we get a yes or a no, and it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I wanted to point at is that whether most of them were seized or not, as the witness says, requires a full knowledge of what happened, including the dark number. I mean, those who have worked in criminal law know that the dark number is one of the most difficult problems to tackle. If you want to explore it, fine. I'm not seeking that. I'm just pointing at what came to my mind when I heard first your question and then the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll explain, through questions, what my point is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, let's take this as an example: If military units, as units, were systematically seizing goods and then taking them back to wherever, warehouses, logistics bases, et cetera, and if you had a suspicion that, in fact, you hadn't been able to take the items that are in their possession, and they drove past the check-points and were storing huge quantities of technical equipment that you didn't get, you would have been obligated to pursue this matter further and go into those units and try to find that material; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we had information that a unit in a particular area has some equipment that are not part of establishment, then the closest military police unit would go there and investigate the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My point, Brigadier Juric, is that as of the 10th of August, in this report, it says that the conclusion was that most of the items had, in fact, been seized at check-points. And my question to you is: As of that time-period, was that consistent with what your conclusion was as to whether or not items had been seized back from any units that may have been involved in looting?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm prepared to move on, unless you have further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't prevent you from moving on at an earlier stage, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- please proceed as you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could have Exhibit P2247 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, please take a look at this report. It's a daily report of the Duty Service of the 72nd Military Police for the 5th of August. Is this the report that you were referring to in your answers to Judge Orie's questions and the questions of the Prosecutor concerning the standard reporting that would go to the military commanders about, for example, the state of crime and disciplinary issues?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is one of the reports that were written up when the new rules on the activity of the military police were adopted, and these were the reports that had to be submitted by commanders to commanders of military districts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is this the type of report that you were referring to in your answers to Judge Orie's questions and the answers of the Prosecutor -- or the questions of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the forms of these daily reports that were sent every day to the command of the military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, and if we could go to the -- first, let's flip through this quickly, but you can see what some of the types of issues are that are reported here, okay, and it talks about threats being made to restaurant owners in Sibenik, "drunken soldier" is in the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn the page in English, please. Violations of military discipline; no events recorded. Sorry, if we could turn the page in Croatian as well. Safety and military road traffic. If we could go to the last page now, please. Second-to-last page, I'm sorry. I'm looking at the addressees on the bottom, and if we could find that as well on the Croatian, please. I'm told that -- and I guess I'll talk to my colleagues in the Prosecution, but the last few pages of the original have not been uploaded into e-court, so we'll rely on the translation here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Bear with me, Brigadier. But the addressees to this daily report on the 5th of August, the first address is the Operative Duty Department of the Military Police Administration. Then it goes to the military district commander. Then it goes to the garrison commander in Split, the SIS, the MUP, chief of Split-Dalmatia police, the Military Court, the Military Prosecutor's Office, et cetera. Now, if you could just note that those are the addressees. So these reports don't just go to the military district commander; they go to a wide variety of addressees, including to the MUP as well. Is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And they went to the Military Police administration; is that your recollection as well?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I won't take you through all the documents now, in the interests of time, Brigadier Juric. But if we were to look at P2248, which is a -- this same type of report for the 6th of August; P2249, which is the same type of report for the 7th of August; P2250, which is the 8th of August; P2251, which is the 9th of August; P2253, which is the 10th of August; none of those reports contain any information about the seizure of the looted items at the check-points that we just went through and explored. In other words, the 5th Company, Sinj, has seized hundreds -- literally hundreds of items at check-points on the 5th, 6th, 7th, and 8th, yet none of that gets reported in the daily reports that go to, amongst others, the military district commander. As the person on the ground there, can you explain to the Trial Chamber why those types of incidents wouldn't exist in a daily report?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really don't know why they were not recorded in a daily report, but it is certain that whatever companies reported on, and in connection with exceptional cases, an officer on my team who covered the work of the crime police, he would have to put that all in a single report and provide this information to whoever he was supposed to report to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Brigadier General Juric, I've now been advised that I've been demoting you several ranks in the Croatian Army, so I apologise. Let me explore that just with you for a moment. General Lausic testified in front of the Trial Chamber, and for the parties, this is P2159 at paragraph 162. When you were -- first let me ask this: Do you recall a meeting on the evening of the 2nd of August where General Lausic spoke to the officers of the Military Police Administration and first told you that you would be going out into the field?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At that time, did he say to you why he wanted you to go out into the field? What was the purpose of having you go out there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking about me, personally, whether he appointed me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No. He established three forward command posts, and my question is: Generally speaking, did he tell you officers, all of you, why he wanted to establish three forward command posts, what was the purpose?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Right now, I cannot answer your question. I don't remember whether he said it specifically in those words. But as I already said, at the moment when he made us aware of this, namely, that certain teams of military police officers were made up in order to be sent to certain locations, he did not elaborate to us why, specifically, we were being sent to these locations. During my testimony yesterday, I said how and in which way I personally accepted that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to continue on this topic, and it might be a good time for a break right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I, in view of what remains -- your time estimate would still be the same, Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will definitely finish well within the second session, maybe by another 45 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, as far as you're concerned, still not more than one session?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I put it actually as perhaps more than one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But I feel we may have a good chance of finishing the witness today, Your Honour, if that helps the Court. I need to know what happens before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mikulicic, are you of the same view, that there's a fair chance --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, the parties tell me that there's a fair chance that we might conclude your testimony today, but Mr. Carrier is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I don't think I will impact finishing today, but I wanted to raise one issue in the absence of the witness just before we break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, perhaps, we'll already ask the witness to be escorted to the place where he, I take it, gets his coffee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: It's a time-saving measure only that we wouldn't have to bring him in and then at the end -- but in anticipation of perhaps Mr. Misetic reading to him portions of General Lausic's testimony and telling him it is General Lausic's testimony, my understanding of the procedure is more in the vein of the Chamber has received evidence that General Lausic reported this or reported that, as opposed to saying what, specifically, one person said. I know that's how Your Honour did it, that's certainly how I've tried to frame mine, so I just wanted to be a peremptory objection if that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, could you please first respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We've been here a long time, Mr. President, so I'm very familiar with the procedure, and that's why you will note that I first asked him what his recollections are of what he was told at the meeting. I tried to get everything in a non-leading way as to what his recollections are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then I may just use a phrase with him, which is that General Lausic not once but at least three times told the Trial Chamber that he wanted his own eyes and ears on the ground. And I simply intend to explore with the witness what he understood by that, if anything, and whether he recalls hearing such a comment from General Lausic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The general guidance is that first it should be explored with the witness, what he knows about the events he's questioned about. Then the second is then that if that is inconsistent with evidence, or seems to be inconsistent with evidence the Chamber heard, that that will then be put to the witness. Now, in a special position where the witness was a subordinate or at least was appointed by a person, it might be wise, and at least I'm glad that Mr. Carrier noted the subtleties in my phrasing of the questions, that to put it perhaps first in terms of, The Chamber received evidence, or, A witness told the Chamber. Now, sometimes, of course, that makes no sense at all, to say, A witness told the Chamber that he had sent you there to be his ears and eyes on the ground, so, therefore, I expect observance of what would provide the best evidence, which is first explore, then put to the witness, in the most appropriate way, what is presented as evidence. That could be directly saying who the witness is. That makes sense sometimes. Sometimes you can take a more cautious approach and not to identify yet the witness who told us these kind of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would be happy to take your guidance if we can consider it over the break. My intention is to say to him that General Lausic -- I mean, phrase it somehow that General Lausic indicated that he was dissatisfied with Operation Flash, in terms of what he -- information he was receiving, and that he wanted his own eyes and ears on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it is clear that we are talking about what moved General Lausic's ears and eyes on the ground, then, of course, it doesn't make that much of a -- doesn't make much sense to say, Well, a witness told us that before he decided whether or not to send additional persons to the ground -- Mr. Carrier, you would agree with me, I take it, in that respect. But, of course, the first question should be, Are you aware of the motives of sending additional persons to the ground. That's, of course, first exploring the knowledge of the witness. And only -- he may say, I know that, because General Lausic wanted to have his ears and eyes on the ground, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's the first point, Mr. President. Just in full transparency, I will now -- you'll recall the discussion yesterday with Mr. Carrier about an order that has not been admitted into evidence yet, that actually went to the witness, about what Mr. Lausic wanted to have reported to him during Operation Storm and afterwards. And I think it's natural to explore with the witness, in light of the questioning about reporting, why General Lausic -- or what his understanding is of why General Lausic would need a separate order itemising the type of information he now wants to receive, if, in fact, for example, these daily reports, which go both to General Lausic and to these various addresses, would have been sufficient. I mean, I think the witness might have some knowledge or understanding for why he's being asked to provide additional information pursuant to an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Carrier, anticipating on questions that he expected you would put to the witness, addressed the Chamber in order to, well, meet, perhaps, some of his concerns, not even knowing yet what the questions are. I think I gave the general basis on which we should proceed, and by the examples I gave, it's also clear that you can't give a once-and-for-all answer to these matters. It also depends on the subject matter. Mr. Misetic, you know that being cautious in this respect, which should not in any way finally affect what you can achieve in cross-examination, saves us a lot -- perhaps a few objections by Mr. Carrier. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And just in that sense of being cautious, the reason I raised it is that at page 34, beginning at line 19, Mr. Misetic prefaced his examination on this point with, General Lausic testified in front of this Chamber, and then referenced his exhibit number and went on. And that's where the concern came from, to even preface before, Such a person has testified before this Chamber, and then to start exploring the areas where that person would be, as Your Honour said, the only source of that type of information, that, I think, perhaps needs to be addressed if there's future reference to witness statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, again it depends on -- if I would say that someone told me that he had given blessing "urbi et orbi" five times in his life, then there's not really a reason, not to say that that was the Pope, because as far as I'm aware of, he's the only one authorised to give this blessing on the St. Peter's Place in Rome. So, therefore, it all depends very much on what the question is, and I think it's clear we should elicit from the witness the evidence, even in cross-examination in the present circumstances, not by already whispering in his ear, Someone with great authority told us this or that. Let's first try to find out what the witness can tell us, and then if there's any reason to put to the witness that others, perhaps even others with great authority, said different things, then we'll do that in the following stages in the -- in such a way that the Chamber is best assisted by the answers of the witness when it will have to make its determinations at a later stage. We have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, the Chamber was informed that you had a certain matter whether or not you would go beyond the scope of cross, as defined by the Chamber. You have approximately said where you may have wanted to go to the Legal Officer of the Chamber. He reported this to the Chamber. The guidance is the same as I gave to Mr. Carrier. It's at the edge. Don't stay too long there, because you could fall off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sir, is the Prosecution going to be informed of what that was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic, the reason why I'm dealing with it in this way is because it prevents us from sending the witness out of the courtroom again, et cetera. Mr. Carrier, if there's at any moment any objection you would like to -- Mr. Misetic was seeking guidance, and you've heard the guidance, that's all; not more, not less. If there's any moment where you think that he goes anywhere where he shouldn't go, then, of course, we'll hear your objection, and then you'll also find out what the guidance was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I understand that, and I appreciate this guidance. I suppose it's in reference to the earlier guidance of the Chamber that it would be sought in written form and to provide notice. That was -- the Prosecution filed a request when Chamber witnesses were initially --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it was credibility, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No, but it was also about whether or not to go outside, there would be notice of what those things were. That was the filing. There was a ruling on that that was put on the record. It was initially in an e-mail, and then it was read into the record. We never had notice of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, of course, the same as this morning, when Mr. Misetic objected to your questions, you had not given notice. But, of course, you considered it not to be outside the scope of. And there's a thin line between that. One of the reasons why I'm dealing with it in this way as well is that it takes usually less time to just proceed, put one or two or three questions. If there's any real concern that you could not have prepared for that, we'll hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: If you could just -- if it could just be e-mailed to us from the Gotovina Defence, what the area is, that would be helpful to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was just about to say, I would just direct my learned friend to transcript page 3786, lines 1 to 9, and transcript page 7653, line 5, to 7654, line 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It must make you happy, Mr. Carrier, to have a lot of numbers. No, no, don't take me serious at this moment. Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Juric, let me call up a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 2193, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You can see, General Juric, that this is an order dated 3rd of August. It is from General Lausic, and you can see the addressees in the upper right-hand corner, it goes to all military police units, including the 72nd. And if we turn the page in English, please. It also goes to the departments and sections of the Military Police Administration. Now, let me first ask you -- and the subject of the report is: "Content of reports on the completion of military police tasks as per the order of the chief of the Military Police Administration, dated 2 August."

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, that is -- and let me just confirm that. I believe that's D267. Yes. D267 is what's referenced there, and that is the order that ordered you to be appointed, and D267 also stated that you would be reporting by 2000 hours, beginning on 4 August. And then this order was issued, describing what the content of the reports should be. Do you recall receiving a copy of this order? And we can turn the page for you in Croatian if you need to see it.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I did receive the order, but I can't be 100 per cent sure. I can't say either, Yes, or, No, for a fact, but I'm -- I believe that I did receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the introduction, General Lausic says that the order is being issued in order to standardise the content of reports on the completion of tasks in the zones of responsibility. And in point 2, if we turn the page in English -- if we can go back in Croatian, please. In point 2, the reports should contain information about the state of law and order in the zone of war operations and in newly liberated areas, listing the incidents in which the military police acted, and the results of the intervention. Point 4, if we turn the page in Croatian, please: "The situation with crime in liberated areas and in the areas in the zone of war operations, the number of crimes processed, criminal reports filed, and HV members, who committed crimes, brought in." And then point 5, which is an area we'll address in a few minutes: "The number of arrested persons by the time of their take-over from HV units, the time of their hand-over to the Reception Centre, the number of civilians, women, children and elderly, handed over to the police stations of the MUP." Now, can you explain what was your understanding of why General Lausic needed to issue an order on the 3rd of August about what information should be contained in reports?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what governed General Lausic in writing this order. I can only speculate. I believe that it was meant to unify the system of reporting and provide all units with a set of guide-lines for uniform reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, would the information that General Lausic seeks in this order already be in the daily reports that we looked at this morning?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, if that were the case, then why would General Lausic need to issue a separate order seeking this information? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that 65 ter 2193 be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D2028.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D2028 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Juric, do you recall anyone at any point indicating to you that you were being sent down there to be a separate set of eyes and ears on the ground?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I note that in General Lausic's orders, it says that where you were, that that was called a forward command post. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What was that a forward command post of?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, is it correct that there were three forward command posts that were established pursuant to General Lausic's orders, one of which was your team, another of which included Colonel Kosic's team, and I can't remember the identity of the third person, but that there were three forward command posts set up?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The chief of the Military Police Administration issued an order to set up three teams that were to cover three different areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And those three teams, they were considered to be forward command posts of the MP Administration; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer your question, sir. I was at the IKM of the commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, and I told you already that I didn't take over the command of the unit. I was attached to the unit as a co-ordinator and as a person who would team up with other professionals and assist the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You see in the order that we just looked at that General Lausic talks about reporting as to civilians that were turned over to the MUP. Can you explain why civilians were being let out of the zone by the military police and turned over to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to answer that question yesterday, and I said that one of the tasks was to do with prisoners of war. Our task was to pull them out from combat-affected areas and hand them over to the civilian police, who had set up accommodation centres for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll just refer the Chamber, then I'll skip this part, to transcript page 13395. It's 13395, line 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention now to your testimony concerning the events in Kistanje. Yesterday, you spoke about encountering some UN personnel from Canada. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, as a preliminary question, did you speak English in 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge, in any form, of English in 1995? Could you understand it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had never learned English before. If I could understand anything, it would be some 50 words that I'd picked up on television and from films.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How did you communicate with these UN officials?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time ever the MPs of the Canadian police came to the building where we were stationed in Knin and asked to meet one of the officers. I was there in the building at that time, and I asked -- I inquired among the MPs if anybody was fluent enough to serve as an interpreter, just to see what the request was. I found somebody, I can't remember his name, and I used him as an interpreter. We managed to establish communication in that way. And our first conversation dealt exclusively with the implementation of the security detail for Mr. Yasushi Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm now specifically referring to this meeting that took place in or around Kistanje on or about the 9th of August, and my question is: At that time on that day, how were you able to communicate with them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was not a meeting. I just happened to be there and come across the patrol of the Canadian MP. It was not a meeting, it was not a conversation, to speak of. We spoke by using hands more than anything else, by using sign language, if you will. So I could understand that they wanted me to call somebody, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did they happen to have an interpreter in their team?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
