utterances.text: Do you recall whether there was any type of question from them concerning the issue of mop-up operations of the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. How could they have asked me anything, knowing that I could not understand English?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll move on, then, from this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Juric, I'd like to show you a video of Kistanje and ask you for your recollections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And this is, Madam Registrar, Exhibit P26. There is no audio, so, therefore, no need for transcripts. And the video will start at the 2 minutes 17 mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. -- General Juric, the Trial Chamber has heard evidence that this video was shot by UN personnel on the 13th of August, and so what I'd like you to do is follow the video. You've already testified, I believe yesterday, that you recall seeing four or five destroyed houses when you were there on the 9th, and I'd like to ask you, to the best of your recollection, if you recognise any of the homes that had been destroyed at the time that you were there. And my first question to you is: If you can look on your screen right now, do you recognise this location just by looking at this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see anything happening. I still have the previous image on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way that we could get this car driving --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I just want to ask him first with respect to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you see a video on your screen right now?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On my screen, I can see the order, the document that we saw previously and commented upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this location?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll play the video, and then I'll ask you a few questions when it stops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Juric, did you recognise anything about that location that we saw on this video?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise the sign posts, and I think -- it seems to me that the sign posts were in the middle of that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: With respect to the -- I think we've seen that at least one building is on fire in this video on the 13th. Can you assist the Trial Chamber, by looking at that scene, as to which buildings may have been burned at the time you were in Kistanje on the 9th and which had not been burned when you were in Kistanje on the 9th?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said yesterday that on the day when I was in Kistanje, I did not see a single building ablaze.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I understand that there was no building on fire at the time that you were in Kistanje. However, were there any buildings that had already been destroyed by fire by the time you got to Kistanje?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that there were four to five buildings that I saw that had been destroyed, but I did not take the trouble to remember where exactly they were, in what micro-locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Juric, thank you for answering my questions. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. Mr. Kay, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, Mr. Kay, who will now cross-examine you, is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry for the delay, Your Honour. I've got a slight technical difficulty. I think that it's all right now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, you answered some questions yesterday from His Honour, and you were asked about what you could tell the Judge on what basis he had a right or authority to issue tasks. And you said that duties, tasks, and whatever the military police had, in keeping with the rules, and every officer had the right to issue requirements and tasks that the military police then implemented if they were in accordance with the area of work. Do you remember saying that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't know whether you can remember the document, but were the rules you referred to there the Rules of Service concerning the military police?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was speaking about the rules on the work and organisation of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And how familiar are you with that document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was affiliated with the military police, I had to know it literally by heart. But as I sit here today, I really don't know how many of the provisions of those rules I could remember off my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I'm going to ask you about is one of the rules - that's Article 73 - and whether that was the rule you were referring to. Can you recollect Article 73 or would you like us to show it to you on the screen, as we have it in court?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please show it to me? I can't remember the specific article without being able to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit P880. And turn to page 28 in the English and page 28 in the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you'd just look at Article 73.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, when you gave that answer yesterday, was that the rule that you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that this was prescribed by articles that deal with the system of command and control of MP units. I don't know what chapter are we reading from. I don't know where the article that we are now looking at is situated, in terms of chapters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. It's the last chapter, actually, in the document. But if it's not that that you were thinking of, we've no need to look at that any further and we can just close that, because that was an article of the rules that we saw there which was a general requirement for all members of the Croatian Army to assist the military police and enable them to gather information and reports. Is that -- am I reading that right, in relation to that article we've just looked at?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without perusing the entire rules on the work and organisation of the military police, I really can't remember the part of those rules that this article is connected to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Okay, very well. You were asked about the right or authority of General Cermak, and you were shown a document today, dated the 3rd of December, 1994, D1280. But there's another document I'd like to refer you to, and that's our Exhibit D34.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if that could be put on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document that concerns the order of organisation and work in the garrisons, and sets out what the garrisons had to do. It's called the organisational order regarding work, order, and discipline, issued on the 27th of August, 1993. Now, in relation to the garrison and the garrison commander, were you familiar with the rules inside this order?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I said yesterday as well that I was not personally familiar with the rules pertaining to the commander of garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to the responsibilities of a garrison commander, would you accept that an order such as this is an order that the garrison commander would have to follow?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this order. I am not familiar with this order. I don't know who wrote it, I don't know who it was issued to, so I cannot interpret it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We should have a look at it. We can see that it's from the Ministry of Defence in Zagreb. We can see the order on page 1. Let us turn now to page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm wondering whether or not this is outside of the scope, given that we're getting into apparently garrison command structure, when the witness has already said he was a member of the military police and doesn't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, it's the fate of all parties to be reminded that you are at the edge. We should avoid that we are seeking legal opinion from witnesses on the basis of documents which they are not familiar with, as they said. So may I ask you not to stay in the danger zone too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm conscious of Your Honour's guidance, but these matters arise from Your Honour's own questioning yesterday on competence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's for other reasons. I would -- as a matter of fact, my concern was perhaps a bit different than Mr. Carrier's, and perhaps it was not fully appropriate not to respond to Mr. Carrier's objections, which is that you went beyond the scope of cross-examination. My concern is slightly different. It is that we are seeking legal opinion from a witness, who doesn't appear as an expert witness, and has several times now told us that he had not looked very much in the -- let's say, in the legal structure of authority underlying the position of Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that begs the question of Your Honour's questions yesterday, to be frank, on the orders. And Your Honour consistently asked about the right of garrison commander, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what I did yesterday is when the witness gave opinions on that, I asked him on what it was based, and whether I would have explored all the legal texts underlying it is a totally different question, Mr. Kay. As you may have noticed, I did not, I didn't take him to that. But since you could suspect that there was some kind of legal opinion in his answers, I'd rather know that than it being -- remaining unknown to me. That's the reason why I asked the questions, which were not given any further follow-up then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I'm not asking for his legal opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I wasn't going to ask his legal opinion, because he'd asked to see who issued the order, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, he said he didn't know who issued the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- if you would please keep in mind what I just said and then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, if you could look at the screen now, please, you'll see that this was issued by the minister of defence, Mr. Susak, as well as the Chief of the Main Staff, General Bobetko. So would you agree, as a member of the armed forces, that this is an authoritative document on the powers of the garrison commander?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, once again, this is the first time I see this document. If it was signed by Gojko Susak, minister of defence, and the Chief of the General Staff, I have no reason to doubt the authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's right. And so in giving your answers to His Honour yesterday concerning the garrison commander, if you were unaware of the powers of the garrison commander, would that affect the accuracy of your answers to His Honour yesterday on certain orders that were described as being issued by General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I said yesterday, in response to every one of your questions, that General Cermak issued tasks, and that we carried out these tasks because all of these tasks were within the scope of work of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, you were on your feet, but you are seated again. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So in relation to what you said yesterday when His Honour described to you some documents issued by General Cermak, would it be right to say that you viewed them as tasks?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that we received tasks from General Cermak, and that within the scope of work and responsibility of military police, we carried them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, if I just look at that, first of all, in respect of those orders, am I right in saying - can you confirm - that you did not recollect any of them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that I had personally seen any one of these orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And would you also confirm that General Cermak never issued any orders to you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that he had never issued any orders to me. Now, whether he gave me some tasks, that is something I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the position is that yesterday, when you were answering His Honour's questions, you were giving your opinion in relation to the matters put to you by the Judge; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, when the Judge was putting to you the descriptions of the documents, which you described as tasks, you were giving your opinion on the competence of General Cermak to have issued such a document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. Kay could point to where it is that the witness described documents as tasks. I'm not familiar where that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, have a look at the transcript. I'm sorry, I'm on my feet, cross-examining, and I don't want to lose my train of thought. Your Honour, this is very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I can't say that I have no concerns, although they are a bit different from Mr. Carrier's. But you may proceed. I'll refrain from any comment at this moment. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is opinion, and what is not opinion, and what is -- that's a matter which is of some concern to me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to His Honour, I gave answers yesterday in the way in which the questions were put to me. If His Honour read certain parts of a document to me, then I would refer, in my answer, to specific questions related to a specific document that His Honour had read out to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would you accept that what His Honour was reading out to you was, in fact, information that was being sent to the military police?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot make decisions here as to whether that is information or whatever, when we are not speaking about a specific document. His Honour, the Judge, read out to me yesterday two or three documents, I believe, or orders. I don't remember how this was exactly formulated. And my answer was exclusively in response to the questions put to me by His Honour. I think that they were in the context of the following: that we, as members of the military police, as we read these documents or orders from General Cermak, we saw what the tasks of the military police were that were prescribed by the rules on the military police, and we carried out those tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you accept that General Cermak could not have ordered you? You decided whether to carry through the task or not.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Cermak was not my immediate superior. It was General Lausic. I said yesterday and I said today that I personally did not see, nor do I remember, any order that General Cermak issued to me personally, or any similar task, for that matter, so I cannot speak about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Aside from your personal position, the Judge's questions yesterday concerned the competence of General Cermak to issue orders to the military police, whether he was competent to do that.

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, once again, General Cermak could give tasks to the military police, and if that task was within the scope of the responsibilities and work of the military police, the military police would carry it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that something that became a task? If he referred to stolen UN vehicles in something called an order, was that information that you received that became a task?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday, I also responded to that question. In this specific case, General Cermak had regular co-ordinating meetings, and he obviously received information about these stolen vehicles. Quite simply, he spelled that information out to us. We understood it to be a task, and we did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the reason it became a task was because you considered that it fell within the scope of your duties as a military policeman?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not because I personally thought that, but because that is what is written in the rules on the work and responsibilities of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If General Cermak had issued something called an order that was not within the duties of the military police, you would have a right to refuse to follow it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a rather hypothetical question. What would happen, had this happened, it depended on the situation involved, on the available number of patrols of the military police, and on what we were doing at that particular point in time. So I cannot give a yes-or-no answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to information provided by General Cermak, the military police had no duty to report back to him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be fair and proper to inform someone who had provided you with some information as to whether you had started doing that or not. However, officially, I don't think that there was any need to report back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could look at a document, please, which is the first one His Honour referred to in evidence, Exhibit D503.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is one of the documents that His Honour was referring to when he was questioning you yesterday. He referred to the 12th of August, and he referred to various vehicles. And in doing so, asked you to comment about that. You said you couldn't remember the order. And what you said of it was: "However, if you say it was drafted, then I'm sure it was." Well, that's what we're -- we're looking at now, Mr. Juric. General Cermak issued a task pursuant to a piece of information that he had received about a crime having been committed and the perpetrators had to be discovered. And in this case, as you've just said, some vehicles had been stolen. This certainly fell within the scope of the work of the military police, and the military police were duty-bound to accept that task and implement that task. And this is what I'm asking you about: that if information was provided to you that was within the scope of your duties, you viewed it as a task?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The fact that this is headed as an order is actually irrelevant to you because it is simply information; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, in your question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your question, you create a causal relationship which is, from a logical point of view, not solid. So whatever the witness answers to it is -- whether something is relevant, because it is simply information, is a double question: Whether it's relevant or not, and the second is why it is relevant or irrelevant. Simply, information, without looking at the document, seems not to be a proper reflection of what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, for the assistance of the Court, I will certainly go back and cover that and make sure that this is considered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The fact that this was headed an order, how did you view that; as an order?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I answered that question yesterday; namely, that it wasn't important how and in which form one of the operative commanders provided something. The essence of the matter is whether it contains what is within the purview of the work of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it's from that, as your duties, that you see your task to go and try and find the vehicles, if you had received this document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can look at the similar one His Honour referred to, D303.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I really have some problems in the way in which you present this document, and I'd like to give a follow-up question to the witness in this respect. Now, you said you felt that you were tasked with finding the missing vehicles, and that was within the purview of your task as the military police. Yes. Now, the document also says that for that purpose, that teams should be formed consisting of members of the MUP and from the Knin Police Station and from the Knin Military Police. Now, if you would have received information, UN vehicles are missing, go and find them, would you have understood that to be that you will be tasked also by setting up such a mixed team, MUP and military police, which had to try to find those vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in principle, all criminal processing that had to do with the work of the crime military police in the field was done jointly together with the members of the civilian police. So regardless of sources of information and regardless of the way in which we received such information, members of the crime military police immediately established direct communication about that with civilian crime police, and then they would start dealing with the matter. We never know whether the perpetrator was a civilian or a soldier, or whether some equipment was hidden by a civilian or a military man. It was a joint effort that was required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is a joint effort and sharing information the same for you as form a team consisting of both elements, that is, MUP and military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that mean that every offence you learned of, and where you were not aware of who the perpetrator was, that you would not seek information in your own teams, your own platoons, but that you would immediately -- apart from sharing information, that you would set up a mixed team?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there is a difference between -- at least from my understanding, but if you take a different view, I'd like to hear from you. There's a difference between working in a team and sharing information with others, and -- well, to see that your work is, well, let's say, co-ordinated to some extent, and making a team consisting of members of two different units. For example, I would understand the one approach to be that you would drive around and try to find those vehicles, but still in your own vehicles, your own team members, whereas a mixed team might be that you have on board MUP people when you are driving around. This is just an example, not to bind you, but just to give you an impression of what I understand to be the difference between working in your own team, sharing information, co-ordinating with teams of the MUP, and forming a team consisting of members of the MUP and the military police. And I explained this to you because my question was that if you would receive information and receive a task that vehicles that may have been stolen should be found, whether you would, under normal circumstances, form a team of mixed composition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Generally speaking, crime military police and crime civilian police, each on its own, would start the proceedings in order to try and detect the perpetrators of such crimes. There would be moments when they would exchange information and update each other on how far they had got. In any case, each of the services would try and find as many elements as possible, and then there would come a time when they would update each other on what they know. The crime police teams did not have to ride on the same team, or inspect the area together, or engage in one and the same search. The two different teams could do it separately, each in their own way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A slight technical difficulty. Just not a great connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From what you're saying, anyone within the armed forces, the Croatian military, was able to pass on information to you about a crime, and you would be duty-bound to look into it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The authorised personnel had to take statement, check the contents thereof, see where there were any elements for further proceedings, and then they would take it from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, again, from any person within the armed forces of whatever rank providing you with information, that was giving you a task if it was about something within the scope of your duties?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the type of information, on the contents thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. If information was passed on to you by a person of any rank within the Croatian armed forces that concerned a matter such as a crime committed by the military that fell within the scope of your duties, that that would be a task?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an expert on the job of the crime military police, but I believe that this is prescribed by the Penal Code of the Republic of Croatia, which clearly describes procedures and the way things are done within the scope of penal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Law on Criminal Procedure?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Articles 139 and 140; is that what you're referring to, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not testing your memory. I was just checking whether that's what you were referring to. I'll try and make the question a bit clearer. If a soldier, not a general, not an officer, had information from the UN that their vehicles had been stolen, and gave that information to the military police, that would then be something they were tasked to deal with?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would have proceeded in the same way as described in the order that we have just seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can now go to Exhibit D303.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is another of the documents that His Honour referred to yesterday, which he described to you, concerning UN vehicles. If you can see it there, it's from the garrison command on the 9th of August, signed by General Cermak. It concerns various vehicles. Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I don't remember ever seeing this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you received this document as an order, would you take it to be an order?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would have considered it a task, one of those that the military police had to discharge, in view that it was about an unlawful misappropriation of somebody's property.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So would it be right to say that the heading being an order is irrelevant to you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that yesterday, in answering the Honourable Judge's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Exhibit D788, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is another of the documents that His Honour referred to yesterday. It concerned controlling entrances to the camp, UN camp. You can see it's dated the 8th of August. His Honour asked you about that. Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: IVAN JURIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether I saw it. I am familiar with what is the subject of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to this as an order, would you view it as an order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, given the line of questioning and the way the questions are being put to the witness, I'm not sure that this is within the scope of the topics, given that I think what he's asking is whether or not Mr. Juric, if he had received these documents, would consider it an order, rather than military police units. There's a difference, and it's important, because Mr. Juric has already explained he's not subordinate to Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, earlier I said that we were at an edge. We're not here at an edge. We're within the territory which is -- which Mr. Kay is entitled to explore. At the same time, the witness testified quite considerably about these matters yesterday, about tasks and orders, and, therefore, to some extent it seems to me to become repetitious, and also it may not that much further assist us. And you may remember, Mr. Kay, that yesterday I relativated [sic] already the order. I always talked about a document which contains the word "Order," or I said something of -- so that may be indicative already, perhaps, for the approach taken. And the witness has explained some matters already three, four, five, or, if not, six times. Would you please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very happy to accept the Court's guidance on that. I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, not to say that there may be not a problem, but what problem is there may not be fully understood by the witness, but is fully understood by the Chamber. Let that be clear. The witness said already how he experienced matters at the time, receiving tasks, feeling, and that's what he said, duty-bound, whatever that finally may mean, whether that is under legal text, or whether he felt it this way, or whether that's what they always did, but for the Chamber the matter is, of course, perfectly clear. And the sole purpose for which I refer to these documents, not even having them on the screen, whether when the witness was talking about tasks, whether these were the kind of things he had on his mind. That is, if that gives further clarification, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm following Your Honour entirely on that. It's just that he didn't feel anything at the time because he didn't receive these. And he said that he was not ordered or tasked by General Cermak, and so I'm slightly confused now with what Your Honour has said about the evidence yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He said that they would receive tasks, and was not specifically referring to these tasks. But that was explored before we went into these documents, and what I -- the only thing I wanted to check with these documents were that these were the kind of things he had on his mind when he said that one would receive -- could receive tasks and that one was duty-bound, then, to do what you were tasked with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is Your Honour saying that -- I don't want to say anything in front of the witness that I shouldn't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps he should take his earphones off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we asked him of his knowledge of the English language at the time, not his present knowledge of the English language. Do you -- have you learned more English since 1995, Mr. Juric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Congratulations with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Probably in the last few days as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I'm also looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Should we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if there's any --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- matter you would like to raise we could do it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I will raise it with Your Honours. It is a matter of great concern to me that I get this right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Preferably, then, before we take the break and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so that we have time to think about it. And, Mr. Juric, Mr. Kay wants to say something in English, although not to be heard by you. It's a procedural matter. Again, could I already invite you to follow the Usher so as to have your coffee first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I'm well aware of the issues Your Honour was dealing with yesterday in relation to tasks, orders, instructions, requests. I noted Your Honour's careful language on that. My concern has been when Your Honour asked about the competence of General Cermak, first of all, and that's something that my learned friend certainly looked at this morning, T-27457. And in using that description, which was not a de facto -- I had -- before we started the witness, I had anticipated Your Honour would be dealing with de facto evidence, to be frank. And when the questioning took this turn, it seemed to me we had moved from de facto to de jure, and that is why I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's, then, misunderstood, Mr. Kay. I can tell you, I never asked the witness whether it was within the competence of Mr. Cermak to do certain things. At least the whole of the context is -- I always asked whether he considered what I was interested to know and to find out yesterday. And if I look at all the places where -- I always said, Did you consider it to be within the competence? And that also explains my question about the legal basis, because apart from always talking in subjective terms in my questions, I also explored whether there was anything more than what he considered, how he perceived it, whether there was a legal basis for that. And I can point you at pages 27459-460. I really always intended to ask him how he perceived it, and I asked him also what -- whether he had any knowledge of a legal basis for that. And I think the answer was, and I don't have that right on my mind at this moment, but that he'd never -- as he told us today several times, he did not inquire into the legal basis for that. So by that, one could establish that the way in which this witness looked at the competence may not have been primarily supported by the legal texts underlying the competence of Mr. Cermak. If you'd carefully look at it, you'll see that it is -- perhaps I may have missed it once, but at least almost always I asked how he considered it. And I did put a question on a legal basis, but since the witness then said, I think, that he had not looked much into that matter, an answer he gave today several times, that's where I left it, and not to explore with the witness what might have been, although he wasn't aware of, the legal basis for what he considered to be the competence. That would be reconstruction afterwards, which I was not that much interested in at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour and I are ad idem on that score, and I was appreciative of the fact of the evidence, that it was not on the basis of something he had done, or seen, or acted upon. But the issue that I was alerted to was, Did you consider this to be a kind of order or giving tasks, as you mentioned before, which was within the competence of Mr. Cermak? And that put me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, again, Did you consider this to be a kind of an order? Did you consider this to be, that's how I meant it. And if that was unclear -- I'll check first with my colleagues whether the way in which I explained to you what was on my mind when I put the questions to the witness, whether that's how they understood it as well, so as to avoid that we have to resolve the matter later among the three of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour, may I say the other reason for my approach as well was because the five orders were listed, and Your Honour went through them, which sent signals to me. I dare say it sent signals to the other side, the Prosecution, as to issues Your Honour might be looking at in this case. So that has been the essence of my approach. This came in as a supplemental, as Your Honour might recall, of exhibits to be adduced, and as soon as my team and I saw that, we thought, Ah, this is now being looked at in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I could give you the very practical reason why it came so late, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not going to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the internal work of the Chamber, but it was of a very practical nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm -- of course. I'm just putting my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, having consulted with my colleagues, I have nothing to add to what I earlier said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Your Honour, if we have the break now, I can just consider carefully what Your Honour has said, the guidance given, and just review my cross-examination as to whether I need go further on matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, having read the matters and considered matters, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Mikulicic, is the position of the Markac Defence still the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have any further questions. Mr. Juric, no one has questions for you anymore. Therefore, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague. I'm glad that we can excuse you before the weekend. I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. [Interpretation] Thank you, goodbye. [In English] May I leave the court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Juric out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any procedural matters which need our attention before the weekend? Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Just to address the -- MFI the Defence exhibit D20 -- I think it's 26 or 27. That was the -- what's described as an Official Note. We've looked at it. It's fine. I know it was going to be briefly MFI'd, but I just wanted to alert you now. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said it is number this or number that. I would like to verify, first of all, which number it exactly is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry, I wrote down "2027," and that's what I was looking at, but I was informed it was 2026. So I might be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the document that was MFI'd, which is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually I believe it is 2027. I believe Mr. Carrier was right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar will have the final word on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D2027 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And just following up on that, I think there was a request for P2247, to have the last two pages updated. We've e-mailed that. I think everyone's in agreement that those should be uploaded, with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because they were not verified. That we worked on the basis of the translation, if at any moment the Defence, because the document was uploaded by the Prosecution, I think, if at any time --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's still a P document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's still a P document. Yes, that's exactly what I meant. If at any moment the Defence would feel that working on the basis of a translation has, in any way, caused confusion or has caused an incorrect understanding of what the document really is, then, of course, we'd like to hear from you as soon as possible. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, finally, whether or not the Chamber's had a chance to consider the map that was tendered today and marked for further identification. The documents that were used to create the map are cited in the document. There's only, I believe, three of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, first of all, that the Defence would look at the map and then inform the Chamber. I think Mr. Kay referred to a different source, which was already indicated in the legenda of the map. Mr. Misetic would like to have a closer look at it, because he had seen it only for a few minutes. Therefore, the Chamber will first receive further submissions, if any, from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we'll take a look at it this weekend, and I'll send an e-mail around by Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then we'll further formalise that in court. Any other matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to avoid whatever confusion, the full document, P2247, is now uploaded, and leave is granted to replace the defective version of this document by the full document. It's only since now we have the two full versions there, that if that, in any way, reveals that the interpretation may not be correct, that we'd then like to hear that. Then we adjourn for the day, and we'll resume Monday, the -- is that -- let me check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the next witness is scheduled for March the 19th, in the afternoon. So we adjourn until Friday, the 19th of March, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. However, I make one observation in this respect, that both from within the Chamber and from Defence counsel of one of the teams, a request has been made to see whether we could swap from afternoon to morning. I already started working on it. I don't want to create any false expectations, because I have already one response of one Presiding Judge, who says, Since I'm sitting both in the morning and the afternoon, there's not a lot to swap. But we'll still have to hear from other Presiding Judges now, two candidates, whether there's any chance that we'll be able to swap. It's -- as I said before, there's a wish both from within the Chamber and from one of the parties. Nevertheless, I can't promise anything, but I'll try to do my utmost best. Then with this on our minds, we'll adjourn, and we'll resume on Friday, the 19th of March, hopefully at 9.00 in the morning, but otherwise at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 19th day of March, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25
